core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Tinea Corporis (Ringworm) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes an evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocol for Tinea Corporis (Ringworm), superficial dermatophyte infection, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: annular scaly red plaque with raised borders on the arm

24M athlete reports a circular, red, scaly skin patch on his left forearm that has been expanding for 2 weeks. The patch has a raised, scaly outer border with a clearer normal-appearing center.
reference_soap.objective: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination. Evaluate for pertinent signs.
reference_soap.assessment: Clinical presentation highly suggestive of Tinea Corporis (Ringworm), superficial dermatophyte infection.
reference_soap.plan: Perform potassium hydroxide (KOH) prep (look for septate hyphae). Prescribe topical Terbinafine or Clotrimazole cream BID for 2 weeks. Avoid topical steroids. Refer to specialty team and provide comprehensive patient counseling.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of Tinea Corporis (Ringworm), superficial dermatophyte infection.
Formulate prioritized differential diagnosis for annular scaly red plaque with raised borders on the arm
Select appropriate laboratory and imaging studies for dermatology
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies for Tinea Corporis (Ringworm), superficial dermatophyte infection.

teaching.one_liner: A superficial dermatophyte fungal infection causing an expanding annular plaque with an active, scaly raised border and central clearing — confirmed by KOH prep and treated with topical antifungals, never steroids alone.
red_flags: No improvement (or worsening) after appropriate topical antifungal therapy — reconsider the diagnosis or ask about prior topical steroid use masking findings
Deep, boggy, follicular nodules (Majocchi granuloma) — needs oral antifungal therapy
Widespread or recurrent disease — screen for diabetes or immunocompromise

history.answer: I noticed a round red rash on my left forearm about two weeks ago, and it has been slowly spreading outward.
It started two weeks ago as a tiny red spot and has gradually enlarged into a ring.
It is only on the inside of my left forearm. There are no other spots anywhere else on my body.
It forms a circle with a raised, reddish, flaky border, while the center looks almost like normal skin.
It itches a little bit, particularly after I get sweaty at practice, but it does not hurt or burn.
No, it stays right there on my arm and does not fade away or move to other spots.
I have never had anything like this happen to my skin before.
No fever, chills, fatigue, or generalized body aches at all.
No sores, ulcers, or irritation inside my mouth, eyes, or private areas.
No, my skin is not peeling off or blistering, and I have no dark purple spots.
No swelling of my lips or face, and no trouble breathing, throat tightness, or dizziness.
I have not started any new prescription pills, antibiotics, or pain medicines.
No new soaps, detergents, skin lotions, or metal jewelry have touched my arm.
A couple of guys on my wrestling team had similar circular itchy spots a few weeks back.
I wrestle on the gym mats almost every day, but I have not been out hiking or bitten by ticks or bugs.
I have never had eczema, asthma, or hay fever.
My joints feel fine, and my fingernails and toenails look totally normal without any pits or discoloration.
I have not applied any creams, hydrocortisone, or antifungal ointments yet because I wanted a doctor to look at it first.
I am in a monogamous relationship, and neither of us has ever had any genital sores or ulcers.
I think I might have caught ringworm from the wrestling mats or someone at the gym.
I am really worried that I might spread it to my teammates during contact practice.
I am hoping you can prescribe an antifungal ointment so it clears up fast and I can practice again.
I have never had any major medical illnesses or chronic conditions.
I have never had surgery and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I do not take any prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or dietary supplements.
I do not have any allergies to medications or foods.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any nicotine or vape products.
I only drink a beer socially once or twice a month, never heavily.
I am a college student and varsity wrestler living in a student apartment on campus.
Nobody in my family has psoriasis, eczema, or other recurrent skin conditions.

exam.finding: Well-nourished, athletic young man in no acute distress.
Blood pressure 120/78 mmHg, pulse 68 bpm, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, temperature 36.7 C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.

Single 4-centimeter circular erythematous annular plaque on the volar left forearm with a raised scaly active border and central clearing; no follicular nodules, crusting, or secondary lesions on the trunk, scalp, or interdigital spaces.
Conjunctivae pink and sclerae anicteric without injection, discharge, or lesions.
Oral mucosa pink and moist without erythema, erosions, or ulcerations.
No palpable cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.
No swelling, warmth, or tenderness in the wrists, elbows, or hand joints.
